claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
The starting alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and undergoes brittle failure.
Dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries cause local stress concentrations and brittle failure in the starting alloy.
Rapid, short-duration annealing can modify the sharp interphase boundaries in the alloy.
Rapid, short-duration annealing can increase room-temperature tensile ductility.
Rapid, short-duration annealing can retain or increase the alloy's strength.
An annealing temperature and duration can be selected that induce limited interfacial atomic diffusion without significant phase coarsening or loss of the lamellar architecture.
The proposed annealing treatment will produce slightly diffused, more coherent interphase boundaries with reduced compositional or morphological gradients.
Short-time annealing promotes limited atomic reordering at the interfaces.
Less abrupt and more coherent interphase boundaries reduce local stress concentration.
More coherent interphase boundaries facilitate dislocation transmission across lamellae.
Dislocation transmission through coherent lamellae can accommodate large local shear without crack formation and alleviate stress concentration.
Preserving the dual-phase lamellar structure will preserve its contribution to high strength.
The treated alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy's yield strength will be maintained or slightly increased relative to the untreated alloy.
Annealing will mitigate interfacial dislocation pile-ups and delay microcrack formation and catastrophic failure.
Excessive annealing temperature or duration may coarsen or homogenize the dual-phase lamellar structure and adversely affect strength.
The proposed benefit is expected during room-temperature tensile loading.
